introduction: A questioner asks why unseen forces are allowed to control a person’s affairs, and is told that they are not. The readings that follow sort a whole vocabulary: the evil eye is superstition, and its effect lies in the soul that fears it; “jinn” means hidden forces, and the popular ghouls are fantasy; the wicked dead have no power over the living; Satan is the lower nature; and whoever is seized by an imagined devil should call on God and wake. Cassius, Epictetus and Proverbs say the same of fate, of things and of fear. The Gospel says evil comes from within. But the New Testament also speaks of principalities and powers and of an adversary who walks about like a lion, and Saul went to Endor. Those passages are placed here in contrast, because the readings ask believers in them to understand them anew.
questions: “The effect lies in the souls, not in the glances.” What does this explanation leave real about the evil eye, and what does it remove?
Paul wrestles with “principalities and powers”, and Peter warns of a roaring lion. How do readings 4, 6 and 11 propose that such language be read?
If Satan is “the lower nature in man”, is the struggle with evil made easier or harder?
Reading 12 gives a practice for someone overcome by an imagined Satan. Why a practice, and not only an argument?

outside.why: Why should unseen forces control one’s affairs? The reading denies that they do. Cassius: the fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, but in ourselves.

Paul writes as one who believes in such forces: we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. How would the readings ask a Christian to hear this verse?
The evil eye is superstition: “the effect lies in the souls, not in the glances”. Epictetus: men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.
Fear does the work that the eye is blamed for. The wicked flee when no man pursueth: but the righteous are bold as a lion.
The reading interprets this verse: ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do. It takes “devil” for a name of what they chose to be.
What the scriptures say of jinn has meaning; what is in common mouths is fantasy. Bacon on superstition: it were better to have no opinion of God at all than such an opinion as is unworthy of him.
How can evil spirits of the dead have influence? The Preacher: the dead know not any thing; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun.

No power is exercised by the evil dead. Saul, in despair, sought out a woman that had a familiar spirit and asked her to bring up Samuel. Scripture tells the story, and condemns the seeking. What does the condemnation itself assume?
“There are no earthbound souls.” In the parable the dead are carried elsewhere, and a great gulf is fixed between the places.
Satan “refers to the lower nature in man”. Jesus: from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts; all these evil things come from within, and defile the man.
Dostoevsky’s Dmitri: God and the devil are fighting there, and the battlefield is the heart of man.

Peter: be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. An adversary without is easier to resist than a nature within. What is gained, and what is lost, by the readings’ translation of the one into the other?
When imagination overpowers, let her call on God and turn upward. God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind.
